subject: machine-learning
question: Does this cross-validation give a reliable recall estimate?

artifact.setup:
Rare-disease data: 1,000 patients, 8 positives, sorted by hospital.
cv = KFold(n_splits=10)   # no shuffling, not stratified
Per-fold recall is averaged to report the model's recall.

ai_claim: Yes. 10-fold cross-validation uses every patient for validation once, so the average recall is reliable.

ai_solution.text: Each patient is in exactly one validation fold.
So the average recall is reliable.

failure.misconception: Using unstratified folds with a rare class
failure.explanation: With 8 positives in 10 folds, at least 2 folds contain no positives at all, and recall is undefined there (0/0); with sorted data, positives may cluster into one or two folds. Averages over such folds are meaningless or dominated by a handful of cases. Use StratifiedKFold (shuffled), fewer folds, repeated CV, and pool predictions across folds before computing recall.
failure.why_convincing: Cross-validation is the standard answer to 'how reliable is this estimate?'.

canonical_solution: No: some folds have no positives, making per-fold recall undefined. Stratify, shuffle, and pool predictions.

valid_evidence.summary: 8 positives in 10 folds: at least 10 - 8 = 2 folds have none.
With the sorted data, 7 of the 8 positives fall into folds 3 and 4.

counterexamples: A fold with zero positives has undefined recall.

hints.text: Count how many positives each fold can have.
Step 2 assumes every fold can be scored for recall.
Stratified folds keep the class ratio in each fold.
Step 2 is wrong: some folds have no positives. Use StratifiedKFold.

repair: Use `StratifiedKFold(n_splits=4, shuffle=True)` (or repeated), and compute recall on pooled out-of-fold predictions.
debrief: Cross-validation inherits the problems of its folds. With rare classes, stratification and pooling are essential.

subject: machine-learning
question: Is the AI's summary of these results correct?
ai_claim: Yes. The model's expected AUC is about 0.82, and the fold-to-fold spread (about 0.03) shows how much the estimate depends on which data it is tested on; a new model would need to beat 0.82 by more than this noise to be clearly better.

ai_solution.text: The mean of the five folds is 0.820.
The standard deviation across folds is 0.029.
The spread reflects variation due to the particular split.
Differences between models smaller than this spread are not convincing on their own.

canonical_solution: Correct. Reporting the mean with its spread (or a paired comparison across the same folds) is the honest summary of CV results.

hints.text: Compute the mean of the five folds.
Step 4 uses the spread to judge differences.
CV scores vary by fold; the spread shows estimate uncertainty.
Compare the spread with a 0.005 improvement.
This solution is correct. Mean and spread are read properly. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: A single CV number hides its uncertainty. Report the spread, and compare models on the same folds.

subject: machine-learning
question: Is model B better than model A?

artifact.note: It is not recorded whether A and B were evaluated on the same fold splits.

ai_claim: Yes. B's mean AUC (0.846) is higher than A's (0.841), so B is the better model.
missing_information: A per-fold, paired comparison. The 0.005 difference is small relative to the 0.02 fold-to-fold spread. If both models used the same folds, the per-fold differences might show B winning consistently (a real, small gain); if B lost on some folds, or the folds differed, the difference is noise.
resolving_scenarios: Same folds, and B beats A on all 5 folds by 0.004-0.006: the small improvement is consistent and likely real.
Different folds (or B wins 3 and loses 2): the 0.005 gap is within noise, and neither is shown to be better.
canonical_solution: The summary statistics cannot settle it. Step 3 compares means without accounting for variation or pairing.

valid_evidence.summary: The difference, 0.005, is a quarter of the fold standard deviation, 0.02.

counterexamples: With different fold splits, the order of the means could reverse on rerun.

hints.text: Compare the gap with the spread.
Paired, per-fold comparisons reduce noise from the data split.
Ask whether the folds were the same.
Step 3 ignores variation. Consistent per-fold wins would support B; otherwise it is noise. It cannot be decided.

repair: Evaluate both models on identical folds (repeated CV) and compare per-fold differences.
debrief: Small differences need paired evidence. The same folds for every model turn a noisy comparison into a sensitive one.
